unit.title: Forces and magnets
unit.blurb: Pushes and pulls, gravity, friction, magnets and magnetic materials.

O1.t: Know that a force is a push or a pull, what forces can do, and that a forcemeter measures forces.

O2.t: Know that gravity pulls things down towards the Earth.

O3.t: Know that friction slows things down, and is bigger on rough surfaces.

O4.t: Know that magnets attract and repel, and have north and south poles.

O5.t: Sort materials into magnetic and non-magnetic, and know that not all metals are magnetic.

captions: Hello, little scientists!
How do we make things move? With forces!
This is lesson 5.1: forces and forcemeters.
A force is a push or a pull.
You push a shopping trolley.
You push a door to close it.
When you kick a ball, that is a push too!
Now let's pull!
You pull a door to open it.
In tug of war, everyone pulls the rope.
And a dog pulls on its lead. Come on, let's go!
Pause and think.
When you open a drawer, is that a push or a pull?
Forces can do lots of things.
They can make things start moving, and stop moving.
They can make things change direction.
And they can change the shape of things. Squash some play dough!
We can measure forces with a forcemeter.
A forcemeter has a spring and a hook inside.
Hook on a bag and pull. The spring stretches.
Read the number. A big pull gives a big number!
Did you know?
Ants are tiny, but very strong.
An ant can pull things much heavier than itself!
Joke time!
Why did the door go to school?
To learn about push and pull!
Your turn.
Which one is a push?
Let's go on a push or pull hunt!
Walk round your home, and open and close things.
Doors, drawers, the fridge, a tap. Is each one a push or a pull?
Make two lists: pushes and pulls.
Let's remember.
A force is a push or a pull.
Forces can make things move, stop, or change direction.
Forces can change the shape of things.
And a forcemeter measures forces. Forceful work!

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Why do things always fall down? Let's find out!
This is lesson 5.2: gravity.
Throw a ball up into the air.
Up, up, up it goes.
It stops for a moment at the top.
Then down it comes! Why does it always come back down?
The Earth pulls everything towards it.
This pull is a force called gravity.
Gravity makes an apple fall from a tree.
It makes rain fall from the clouds, and it keeps your feet on the ground!
Pause and think.
What force pulls things down to the ground?
Gravity is everywhere.
Rain falls down.
You slide down a slide.
Autumn leaves fall. Water runs downhill. That is all gravity!
Far out in space, astronauts float about.
On the Moon, gravity is much weaker than on the Earth.
Astronauts on the Moon can jump very high!
Boing!
Did you know?
On the Moon, you could jump about six times higher than you can on the Earth!
Joke time!
Why are gravity jokes so funny?
Because they really get you down!
Your turn.
What happens to a ball when you let go of it?
Let's do a drop test.
Hold a ball in one hand and a flat sheet of paper in the other.
Drop them at the same time. Which one lands first?
Now scrunch the paper into a ball, and try again. What happens?
Let's remember.
Gravity is a pulling force.
The Earth's gravity pulls things down towards the ground.
It keeps our feet on the ground.
And on the Moon, gravity is weaker. Down-to-earth work!

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Why do things slow down and stop? Let's find out!
This is lesson 5.3: friction.
Roll a ball across the grass.
It rolls, and rolls, and slows down.
Then it stops.
Something is slowing it down. That something is a force called friction!
Friction happens when two surfaces rub together.
Smooth surfaces, like ice, have very little friction. Things slide easily!
Rough surfaces, like carpet, have lots of friction.
Things slow down quickly on rough surfaces.
Pause and think.
Which surface has the most friction?
Friction is very useful.
The bumpy bottoms of your shoes grip the floor, so you do not slip.
Bike brakes rub on the wheels to stop the bike.
And friction helps you hold your pencil!
Try this! Rub your hands together fast.
Rub, rub, rub!
Feel them now. They are warm!
Friction makes heat. That is why we rub our hands on a cold day.
Did you know?
Ice skaters can glide very fast.
That is because ice is so smooth. There is very little friction!
Joke time!
Why did the banana skin go to the party?
Because it was a slippery dancer!
Your turn.
Why do shoes have bumpy bottoms?
Let's have a ramp race!
Lean a board on some books to make a ramp. Let a toy car roll down it.
Now cover the ramp with a towel.
Roll the car again. Which one was faster? Which had more friction?
Let's remember.
Friction is a force that slows things down.
Rough surfaces have lots of friction.
Smooth surfaces, like ice, have little friction.
And friction helps our shoes grip the floor. Smooth work!

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Magnets can pull things without touching them! Let's explore.
This is lesson 5.4: amazing magnets.
Here is a magnet.
Hold it near a paper clip.
Click! The paper clip jumps onto the magnet!
The magnet pulls the clip. We say the magnet attracts it.
A magnet has two ends.
We call them the north pole and the south pole.
The poles are the strongest parts of the magnet.
They pull the hardest!
Pause and think.
What does attract mean?
What happens when two magnets meet?
A north pole and a south pole attract. They snap together!
Two north poles push each other away. We say they repel.
Two south poles repel too. Try it, and feel the push!
We use magnets every day.
Fridge magnets hold up pictures.
There is a magnet in the fridge door, so it stays shut.
And a compass needle is a tiny magnet that points north!
Did you know?
The whole Earth is like a giant magnet!
That is why a compass always points north.
Joke time!
What did the paper clip say to the magnet?
I find you very attractive!
Your turn.
What happens when two north poles meet?
Let's go magnet fishing!
Cut out some paper fish, and put a paper clip on each one.
Tie a magnet to a string, and tie the string to a stick.
Now dangle your magnet. How many fish can you catch?
Let's remember.
A magnet can pull some things towards it. We say it attracts them.
A magnet has a north pole and a south pole.
Different poles attract.
The same poles repel. Magnetic work!

q.prompt: Which one will stick to a magnet?

stops.note: Paused on the “Pause and think” card.

options.fb: Gold and aluminium are not magnetic.

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Does a magnet stick to everything? Let's test it!
This is lesson 5.5: magnetic materials.
Let's test things with a magnet.
Try a steel spoon. It sticks!
Try a teddy. It does not stick.
Things that stick to a magnet are magnetic.
Iron is magnetic.
Steel is made from iron, so steel is magnetic too.
Steel nails, paper clips and steel food cans stick to magnets.
Click, click, click!
Pause and think.
Which one will stick to a magnet?
Lots of things are not magnetic.
Wood, plastic and paper do not stick.
Glass and rubber do not stick.
And here is a surprise: most metals are not magnetic! Aluminium cans and gold do not stick.
Magnets can pull through some materials.
Put a sheet of paper between a magnet and a paper clip.
The magnet still pulls the clip!
It can even pull through water. Amazing!
Did you know?
Recycling centres use giant magnets.
They pull steel cans out of the rubbish, so the steel can be used again!
Joke time!
Why was the magnet so popular at school?
Because everyone was attracted to it!
Your turn.
Are all metals magnetic?
Let's do a magnet sort!
Collect ten small things: a key, a coin, a pencil, a sock, a spoon.
Guess first: will it stick? Then test it with a magnet.
Sort them into magnetic and not magnetic. Were your guesses right?
Let's remember.
Magnetic materials stick to a magnet.
Iron and steel are magnetic.
Wood, plastic and paper are not magnetic.
And not all metals are magnetic. Attractive work!
